```json
{
  "body": "Treat this as three separate problems wearing one coat. The first is memory: two people can honestly recall the same conversation differently, and each retelling hardens the divergence. The fix is unglamorous — after any agreement, write it down in one shared place (a note on the fridge, a pinned group-chat message, a shared doc) with three items only: the task, whose it is, and when or by when. This doesn't signal distrust; it removes the recurring argument about what was said, and it works best if you frame it that way rather than as evidence-gathering.

The second problem is definition. Many chore disputes are really about what "done" means — one person's "cleaned the kitchen" includes wiping counters, the other's doesn't. For the handful of recurring tasks, agree a concrete finish line once, in the same written place. It feels pedantic the first time and saves every later round.

The third problem is that your system is brittle to changing schedules. Don't assign chores to fixed days; assign them to conditions or windows ("bins out before Thursday morning collection, owner X; if X is on nights, they arrange a swap and say so"). Then review briefly rather than renegotiating constantly: a fixed 10–15 minute check-in once a week with a set agenda — what got missed, what changed in schedules, any swaps. Long open-ended talks are exactly the format your avoiding friend is fleeing.

On the avoidance: don't chase them into the format that already failed, and don't interpret it as not caring. It more often means the conversations have become punishing — too long, circular, or felt like blame. The way back is a low-stakes invitation: say you want one conversation about *how* you'll decide these things, not about the chores themselves, ask what would make the talks bearable, and actually shorten them afterwards. If they won't engage even with that, propose a one-month trial of the write-it-down system where participation costs them almost nothing, and let results make the case.

One calibration: aim for "fair enough over time," not exact weekly equality. Precise scorekeeping breeds the very resentment it's meant to prevent. If a month of structure changes nothing, the issue is probably less about chores than about something underneath it — that's a different conversation, and a rarer, bigger one.",
  "commitments": "Taking this up commits the household to a few concrete behaviours, not to agreeing with my diagnosis. Maintaining a single shared written record after each agreement, plus explicit definitions of done for recurring tasks — that is the load-bearing part, and it only works if all three treat it as a memory aid rather than a dossier; the record itself can become ammunition if used to score points, which is a real risk I flag rather than solve. Setting and protecting a short weekly check-in, and the inviter specifically shortening conversations after asking the avoiding friend what would help — the advice about avoidance depends on that follow-through. Tolerating approximate fairness is a scope choice, not a finding; if the underlying grievance is about respect or money rather than tasks, this system will paper over it and my recommendations should be revised. The one-month trial is a proposed test, and I am proposing it fallibly: persistent avoidance or escalation despite the structure would count against my claim that this is mainly a coordination problem, not confirm it. If one flatmate refuses even the trial, only the unilateral parts remain available to the asker — confirming agreements in writing, stating their own standards, attending to tone — and I cannot claim those alone resolve a three-person dispute. Unresolved: what to do when the avoiding friend also avoids the meta-conversation, which this account does not cover."
}
```
